A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same INFORM study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and matchable, including material reorganized between versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, training dynamics, attribution analyses, perturbation experiments, and masking ablations on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MMLU.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds perturbation performance, token costs, inference-time measurements, individual-expert scores, and encoder/pooling robustness results.

M1.justification: The canonical orchestrator, interaction and selection modules, gradient attribution formula, training losses, and adaptive sparsity mechanism remain unchanged. Alternative encoders and pooling strategies are evaluated as robustness variants rather than replacing the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K, HumanEval, and MMLU, homogeneous and heterogeneous expert pools, the same four prompt perturbations, and a confidence-based cascade setting. New measurements and model configurations do not introduce additional datasets or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds a sequential inference comparator in the new latency comparison in Appendix G.2 and Figure 16. MetaGPT, the existing standalone and monolithic model comparators, and the original routing-ablation comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Section 4 changes the stated expert-output prefix supplied to the orchestrator from 512 to 30 tokens, without establishing whether retained experiments were rerun. Added evaluation designs measure perturbation accuracy and output-token counts, latency across 2–10 experts, and encoder/pooling sensitivity using fixed input samples.

E4.justification: Appendix M adds controlled encoder and pooling ablations testing whether attribution rankings depend on representation choices. Existing perturbation and masking analyses gain task-performance and token-cost outcomes; heterogeneous attribution heatmaps and computational-overhead analysis further expand the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Three-run reporting for static ablations, epoch-based confidence intervals and standard deviations, and paired Wilcoxon and t-tests are retained. Appendix M adds results using existing rank-correlation measures, without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation practice or specifying additional repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: Matched original numerical results are retained, but substantial results are added. Table 7 adds masked-task scores of 70.9, 76.9, and 85.0 for GSM8K, MMLU, and HumanEval. Tables 11–14 add standalone expert scores and representation-robustness results, including Spearman correlations of 0.84–0.95. New plots report perturbation accuracy, token costs, heterogeneous attribution, and latency.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of routing, intrinsic importance, training objectives, and cascade stopping sensitivity are unchanged. No theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is added; qualifications about causality concern interpretation rather than revised mathematics.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, research questions, and conclusion replace causal-attribution framing with intrinsic or functional attribution and explicitly limit gradients to local sensitivity. This calibrates the advertised contribution while retaining the main findings; v1 already disclaimed formal causal guarantees in Appendix A.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting perturbations to verbosity and accuracy degradation, heterogeneous routing to distributed intrinsic influence, and representation tests to attribution stability. It expands failure-mode explanations and clarifies that experts may be black boxes while the orchestrator must be accessible. New limitations identify untested decentralized, emergent-communication, and reinforcement-learning orchestration regimes.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code link, exact role prompts for the MetaGPT comparison, and a statement that token budgets are matched per instance and role. It also documents configurations for the new representation experiments. However, Table 11's purported consortium baselines use model counts and temperatures inconsistent with Table 6, limiting reproducibility.

R1.justification: The cited works and comparison landscape remain unchanged. Table 1 and the related-work discussion refine INFORM's distinguishing contribution from causal interpretability to gradient-based functional attribution, modestly narrowing its positioning relative to existing routing frameworks.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title and attribution terminology, edits introductory passages, expands explanatory examples, and consolidates the main-text takeaway boxes into Appendix A.2. The principal section sequence and analytical narrative remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn. Earlier Figures 6–7 become combined Figure 8, and Tables 6–7 become Table 6's two panels. New perturbation, heterogeneous-attribution, and latency figures, an expanded masking table, and new baseline, robustness, and prompt tables substantially extend the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 brings prominent claims closer to v1's existing causal caveat, adds useful task-impact and representation-robustness evidence, and improves documentation through a code pointer and exact comparison prompts. These gains are tempered by the unexplained 512-to-30-token setting revision and the mismatch between Tables 6 and 11's expert configurations. Overall quality improves, but unresolved reproducibility issues limit the gain.
